The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 emphasizes the importance of standards to protect workers from increasing workplace hazards. 9. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) has developed a formal research system to establish valid criteria for effective safety standards. 10. 11. Medical monitoring must be provided to all workers exposed to cadmium, including preplacement examinations for new or reassigned employees. 12.g., BUN, liver enzymes), and urinalysis (e.g., protein determination, specific gravity). 13. Periodic medical examinations should be conducted annually, except for urine protein determinations, which should occur every four months. 14. 15. Engineering controls should be implemented to maintain airborne cadmium concentrations at or below recommended limits. 16. Respirators should only be used during installation/testing of engineering controls, non-routine maintenance, single operations, or emergencies, and must comply with specific selection and usage requirements. 17. Workers must be trained in proper respirator use, fit testing, and maintenance. 18. Work clothing should be exchanged daily to prevent cadmium contamination outside the workplace, and proper laundry procedures must be followed. 19. Sanitation practices should include vacuum or wet cleaning methods to avoid cadmium-containing dust dispersion. 20. Food storage, handling, and consumption must be separated from cadmium work areas, and smoking in cadmium work areas is prohibited. 21. 22. 23. Acute pulmonary effects include dyspnea, cough, and chest tightness, often progressing to pulmonary edema within 24 hours. 24. Chronic renal effects are characterized by proteinuria, particularly low molecular weight proteins, indicating early renal dysfunction. 25. 26. 27.
